t: For three thousand years the peoples of Mesoamerica, from the Olmecs to the Maya and the Aztecs, shared a religion of gods of rain, maize, sun and wind, of sacred mountains and caves, and of time measured by interlocking calendars.

Kings and priests offered the gods incense, their own blood and, at times, human lives in pyramid temples, to repay the gods who, in the myths, had sacrificed themselves to set the sun moving and to create humanity.

Suppressed after the Spanish conquest, it survives in a handful of painted books, the Popol Vuh, the ruins of its temple cities and traditions, such as the 260-day calendar, still kept in Maya communities.
dyk: In 1562 the Franciscan friar Diego de Landa burned the Maya books he found at Maní in Yucatán as works of the devil; only four Maya books survive today, in Dresden, Madrid, Paris and Mexico City.
ev: The Olmec centre of San Lorenzo flourishes on the Gulf Coast of Mexico, with the earliest monumental religious art of Mesoamerica
The Pyramid of the Sun is completed at Teotihuacan, the city the Aztecs later believed to be the birthplace of the sun
Stela 29 is raised at Tikal, the earliest known dated monument of the Maya lowlands
The Mexica found Tenochtitlan, by tradition where their god Huitzilopochtli had promised
The Great Temple of Tenochtitlan is rededicated with the sacrifice of many captives
The fall of Tenochtitlan to the Spanish and their allies ends the Aztec state religion
The friar Diego de Landa burns Maya books and images at Maní in Yucatán
The Spanish take Nojpetén, capital of the Itza, the last independent Maya kingdom

f.origin: Mesoamerica, from central Mexico to Honduras, with the Olmec civilisation from about 1200 BCE
f.founder: None: it was shared and transformed over three thousand years by Olmecs, Zapotecs, Maya, Teotihuacanos, Toltecs, Mixtecs and Aztecs
f.scriptures: Painted screenfold books, of which only a handful survive, such as the Dresden Codex and the Codex Borgia; the Popol Vuh of the K’iche' Maya, written down in the 16th century
f.followers: None as a public religion since the Spanish conquest; Maya day-keepers still count the 260-day calendar, and many old traditions live on within Catholic practice
